assoc.t: oral, the word for spoken or of the mouth
Oral Roberts, televangelist and university founder

e.note: Identical to the word oral, as in oral exam and oral hygiene, which invites jokes.

e.etymology: A respelling of Nancy, a medieval English pet form of Annis (Agnes) that was later attached to Ann, from Hebrew Channah, 'grace'.
A short form of Amanda, a name made in the 1600s from Latin amanda, 'she who must be loved'.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
A feminine spelling of Bobbie, the pet form of Roberta and Barbara. Roberta is the feminine of Robert, from Germanic hrod, 'fame', and beraht, 'bright'.
A feminine elaboration of Arnold with the -etta ending, used in the US in the early 1900s. Arnold comes from Germanic arn, 'eagle', and wald, 'rule'.
A Spanish short form of Brunilda, the Spanish form of Brunhild, from Germanic brun, 'armor', and hild, 'battle'. It is used in Puerto Rico and across Latin America.
A respelling of Tammy, the pet form of Tamara, the Russian form of Hebrew Tamar, 'date palm'. Tammy has also been short for Thomasina.
A short form of Sylvester, from Latin silvestris, 'of the forest', used as a name of its own in the American South around 1900.
A respelling of Bernice, from Berenike, the Macedonian form of Greek Pherenike, 'bringer of victory'. A Bernice appears in the Acts of the Apostles.
An English surname from an Old English nickname meaning 'carefree'. It became a girls' name in the 1940s through Corliss Archer, the teenager of the play Kiss and Tell and a long-running radio show.
In the US, a 1960s name close to Alesia, Lisa and Leticia. Lesia is separately a Ukrainian pet name, known from the poet Lesia Ukrainka.
A respelling of Michelle, the French feminine of Michel (Michael), from Hebrew Mikha'el, the question 'who is like God?'
A transposed spelling of Kathryn found in US records. Kathryn is a form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine, long tied to katharos, 'pure'.
A respelling of Dwayne or Duane, from the Irish surname O Dubhain, 'descendant of Dubhan', a name built on dubh, 'dark, black'.
A respelling of Merry, from the English word, Old English myrige, 'pleasant'. Merry has also been a pet form of Mercy and Meredith.
An older spelling of Maddie, the pet form of Madeline (from Magdalene, 'woman of Magdala'). Around 1900 it also overlapped with Maidie and Mattie.
A respelling of Pamela, which the poet Sir Philip Sidney coined for his romance Arcadia around 1580, probably from Greek pan, 'all', and meli, 'honey'.
A respelling of Ashley, an English surname from places named with Old English aesc, 'ash tree', and leah, 'clearing'. It was a boys' name before it became a top girls' name in the 1980s.
A spelling of Keisha, an African American name from the 1960s that may go back to the biblical Keziah. It can also be a short form of Lakecia and Markecia.
A respelling of Kristin, the Scandinavian form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'. The y borrows from Krystal.
A feminine form of Bernard, from Germanic bern, 'bear', and hard, 'brave, strong'. It also honors St. Bernardine of Siena, a 15th-century Franciscan preacher.
From the nickname Curly, for someone with curly hair, and also from a surname of the same sound. It was a boys' first name in the American South around 1900.
namesakes: Curley (the boss's hot-tempered son in Of Mice and Men)

e.etymology: A spelling of Latisha, the American phonetic form of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, 'joy, gladness'. It also fit in with the La- names of the 1970s.
A spelling of Merle, from French merle, 'blackbird' (Latin merula). Merle has also been used as a variant of Muriel and Meryl. This spelling echoes Myrtle.
A French pet form of Laure (Laura), from Latin laurus, the laurel whose leaves crowned victors in ancient Rome.
A respelling of Natasha, the Russian pet form of Natalya (Natalie), from Latin natale domini, 'the Lord's birthday', that is, Christmas.
A spelling of Merle, from French merle, 'blackbird' (Latin merula). It was used for both boys and girls in the US around 1900.
A spelling of Shawna, the feminine of Shawn, an English spelling of Sean, the Irish form of John. John comes from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
From the Germanic name Haduwig, joining hadu and wig, two words for battle. St. Hedwig of Silesia and the Polish queen Jadwiga carried it; German immigrants brought it to the US.

assoc.t: Hedwig and the Angry Inch, rock musical and film

e.etymology: A short form of Patricia, the feminine of Patrick, from Latin patricius, 'nobleman', a member of Rome's patrician class.
A respelling of Roosevelt, a Dutch surname meaning 'rose field'. It became an American boys' name in honor of President Theodore Roosevelt, and this spelling peaked during his term.

assoc.t: Presidents Theodore and Franklin D. Roosevelt
